title: The songs of whales
text: Among the strange sounds of the ocean, none is more haunting than whale song. Male humpbacks sing elaborate sequences that change over months, until every male in a population is performing the same {{1}} (REVISE) version; when a genuinely new song appears, it can sweep across an entire ocean basin — cultural {{2}} (TRANSMIT) on a massive scale, and once thought to be an exclusively human phenomenon. Sperm whales, meanwhile, exchange short patterned clicks known as codas. Families carry {{3}} (REGION) dialects, and some units of sound are shared across thousands of kilometres, implying a degree of social {{4}} (COHESIVE) that surprised the researchers who first mapped it. Whether all this amounts to language in the full sense remains {{5}} (DISPUTE), but its {{6}} (COMPLEX) is not in serious doubt. What is harder to dispute is the damage we have caused: in some waters, ship strikes now kill more whales than whaling ever did, and the constant roar of propellers can leave animals {{7}} (EFFECT) deaf in the very channels they use to find one another. Encouragingly, some ports have begun creating quiet shipping lanes — conservation that protects not merely whales but their {{8}} (COMMUNICATE) itself.

'cultural transmission on a massive scale' — noun from transmit.
'a degree of social cohesion' — noun from cohesive.
'its complexity is not in doubt' — noun from complex.
'leave animals effectively deaf' — adverb from effective.
